question: Where is the industry heading on fee structures and pricing transparency?

claims.text: McKinsey (PriceMetrix research, February 10, 2025) reports that after a period of fee compression for advisory relationships from 2013 to 2018, advisory fee rates have stabilized.
McKinsey (April 8, 2026) states it believes fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

Deloitte (May 20, 2026) states that while lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.

Edward Jones's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that significant reductions in mutual fund and insurance revenues are driven in large part by the ongoing fee compression that has occurred across the mutual fund industry in recent years.
Cerulli (May 28, 2025) states that for the past decade, financial firms have shifted their compensation models from largely commission-based to an asset-related fee structure.
Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.
Cerulli (April 9, 2026) attributes the increased willingness to pay for advice in part to continued fee compression across both advisors and product fees.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that the market environment in recent years has resulted in a shift to passive investment products, which generate lower fees than actively managed products.
A Wealthtender survey (August 13, 2025) found that nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility.

Industry trade coverage (September 30, 2026) states that the broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue, with the SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures and litigation over client yields.

McKinsey (April 8, 2026) reports that industry leaders are worried whether the rapid commoditization of technical expertise will erode the barriers to entry that have historically protected high-margin advisory fees.

Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports an industry-wide shift to data fees and ETF platform/revenue-sharing fees, with Fidelity introducing a $100 ticket charge in March 2024 on trades of funds that refused to pay shelf-space fees, and UBS and Wells Fargo introducing data fees in the mid-2010s and 2020 respectively; an analyst predicted the widespread adoption of data fees to offset declining transaction revenue.

Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Merrill Lynch is creating new data and shelf fees, creating fee bundles on up to $1.4 billion for third-party managers to pay in exchange for getting listed and recommended by its brokers.

McKinsey research (April 8, 2026) holds that if AI collapses the marginal cost of generating tax analysis, scenario modeling, portfolio commentary and meeting documentation, then operating leverage, advisor capacity and fee durability require rigorous reexamination.

Schwab's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it periodically adjusts fees for advisory services, expense ratios on funds/ETFs, trade commission rates and other pricing to sustain its competitive position, citing increased price competition such as reduced commissions, higher deposit rates and reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios.
A survey (August 13, 2025) found just over 38% of people consider lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag when evaluating a financial advisor.
A survey (August 13, 2025) found 'Fee structure and pricing' was cited by 61.8% of respondents as the most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor.

Trade press (September 30, 2026) reports the SEC has focused on cash sweep account options for several years, including a $187 million settlement with Charles Schwab in 2022 over misleading disclosures related to its robo-advisor cash program, and more recently closed its probe into LPL's cash sweep program without enforcement action.

In June 2022 Schwab and its affiliate settled an SEC matter over historical disclosures and marketing of the Schwab Intelligent Portfolios program, with the SEC finding CS&Co. made false and misleading statements about cash allocations, including its conflict of interest and the negative effect of cash allocations on performance.
Schwab (2Q25 earnings call) notes the SEC's decision to lower exchange processing fees beginning in mid-May 2025.
Nearly three-quarters (73%) of survey participants said transparency in fees and services is crucial for establishing an advisor's credibility, according to a Wealthtender survey (August 13, 2025).

Wealthtender (August 13, 2025) reports that AI tools like ChatGPT also prioritize clear, verifiable fee disclosures when evaluating an advisor's reputation, treating ambiguity in fees as a red flag for trustworthiness.
Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (October 9, 2025) reports that wealthy next-generation (generation X, Y, and Z) high-net-worth households seek transparency in advisor compensation.
McKinsey (April 8, 2026) expects fee pressure to be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that in fixed income and equity markets, regulatory requirements have resulted in greater price transparency, leading to price competition and decreased trading margins.

The SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures, combined with litigation over allegedly low client yields, means cash sweep transparency and pricing remains a live issue for advisors, per trade coverage (September 30, 2026).

Sources (September 29, 2026) state platform tolls (data fees and support fees) showing up at the large distributors are directly or indirectly traceable to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry.

McKinsey (February 10, 2025) reports that almost 80 percent of affluent households surveyed indicate they would rather pay a premium of 50 basis points or more for human advice than use a customized digital advice service priced at about ten basis points.
Vanguard research (June 4, 2025) reports that for digital advice, key attributes clients seek include an awareness of fees, alongside transparency of portfolio changes and constant plan monitoring.
Deloitte (May 20, 2026) states that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare.
Wealthtender's advisor-search study (July 2025) found that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when evaluating financial advisors.
The Wealthtender study (August 13, 2025) reports that many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, which the study describes as creating an opportunity for transparent advisors.

A Wealthtender survey (2025) found that nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over another.
The Wealthtender study (2025) identifies fee transparency as a competitive advantage (73% priority), noting that clear fee communication is a powerful differentiator.
The Wealthtender study (2025) recommends that advisors prioritize fee transparency (73% priority) by ensuring pricing is clearly communicated across all marketing materials.
A survey of consumers (August 13, 2025) found that just over 38% consider a lack of transparency about fees or commissions a major red flag when hiring a financial advisor.
Schwab President and CEO Rick Wurster (2Q25 earnings call, July 18, 2025) said the firm wants to work alongside regulators in a way that creates transparency, low-cost, effective markets.
Edward Jones (trade coverage, September 30, 2026) said RPAG will provide benchmarking, fee comparisons and ongoing management of workplace retirement plans.

Morgan Stanley Wealth Management's brochure (November 4, 2026) discloses that clients may be assessed trading-related costs (mark-ups, mark-downs and/or other fees and charges) by another broker-dealer, in addition to program fees.

Morgan Stanley's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that the SEC's Regulation Best Interest requires broker-dealers to act in the best interest of retail customers at the time a recommendation is made without placing the financial or other interests of the broker-dealer ahead of the interest of the retail customer. Why it might matter: the source states MSSB's advisory-client relationships are subject to fiduciary and other obligations, and that the SEC and other supervisory bodies have broad administrative powers to address non-compliance, including restricting MSSB from carrying on investment advisory and asset management activities.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that under the Dodd-Frank Act the SEC adopted Regulation Best Interest, which requires a broker-dealer to act in the best interest of a retail client when making a recommendation, and Form CRS, which requires retail investors be given a brief summary document with information about the relationship, and that various states have proposed or adopted laws imposing new standards of conduct on broker-dealers. Why it might matter: the passage describes a package of rule-makings and interpretations related to the provision of advice by broker-dealers and investment advisers, including Regulation Best Interest and Form CRS.

Edward Jones's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it is subject to the SEC rule requiring registered investment advisers and broker-dealers to deliver a Form CRS Relationship Summary informing clients of the types of relationships offered, the applicable standards of care, and information on fees, costs, conflicts of interest, and legal and disciplinary history. Why it might matter: the passage notes the SEC has also issued guidance establishing a standard of care for broker-dealers that includes acting in the best interest of brokerage clients when making a recommendation and addressing conflicts of interest.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that in April 2024 the Department of Labor issued a final rule significantly expanding the definition of investment advice fiduciary under ERISA and finalized amendments to several class prohibited transaction exemptions that exempt certain compensation arrangements otherwise prohibited, and that if the rules become effective compliance will require altering certain business practices and imposing additional costs. Why it might matter: the passage notes the UK Consumer Duty requires firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers with respect to products and services, price and value, consumer understanding, and consumer support.

Schwab's 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that in March 2026 federal district courts reached final resolutions on pending litigation and formally vacated the U.S. Department of Labor's April 2024 final rule to broaden the definition of fiduciary under ERISA, and the rule was removed from the Code of Federal Regulations. Why it might matter: the source notes the courts' ruling resulted in the DOL's Employee Benefits Security Administration removing the rule from the Code of Federal Regulations.

Morgan Stanley (ADV, November 4, 2026) states that under Department of Labor regulations under Section 408(b)(2) of ERISA, MSWM is required to provide certain information regarding its services and compensation to assist fiduciaries and plan sponsors in assessing the reasonableness of their plan's contracts or arrangements, including the reasonableness of its compensation. Why it might matter: the passage indicates this information is provided for Retirement Accounts subject to ERISA to help fiduciaries assess the reasonableness of compensation.

Merrill Lynch (ADV, October 30, 2026) states that under Department of Labor regulations under Section 408(b)(2) of ERISA it is required to provide certain information regarding its services and compensation to assist fiduciaries and plan sponsors of retirement accounts subject to ERISA in assessing the reasonableness of compensation. Why it might matter: the passage notes this information is provided at the outset of the relationship through the Retirement Account Addendum/408(b)(2) fee disclosures which references information about compensation.

Raymond James's 10-Q (period ended June 30, 2026) states that beginning in August 2024 the SEC's Division of Enforcement requested information regarding its practices related to cash sweep programs for investment advisory clients, and that class action lawsuits were filed alleging breach of fiduciary duties with regard to rates paid to clients in its cash sweep programs. Why it might matter: regulatory agencies and SROs institute investigations from time to time into industry practices, and the firm has reportedly been subject to similar reviews at other financial institutions.

Trade press (September 30, 2026) reports that the SEC has been focused on cash sweep account options for several years, with sizable settlements including a $187 million agreement with Charles Schwab in 2022 over misleading disclosures related to its robo-advisor cash program, and that the SEC closed its probe into LPL's cash sweep program without enforcement action in January 2026. Why it might matter: the source notes the combination of ongoing litigation and regulatory scrutiny over sweep practices adds a further layer of uncertainty, with balances below the levels that prevailed before the 2022-2023 rate-rise cycle.

Merrill Lynch (ADV, October 30, 2026) states that on April 3, 2023 the SEC issued an administrative order finding MLPF&S violated the Advisers Act because wrap fee advisory program agreements and ADV brochures contained a material misstatement by failing to disclose an additional production credit fee on foreign currency exchanges, resulting in a penalty totaling $9,694,714. Why it might matter: the order additionally found a failure to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations.

Schwab (ADV, October 15, 2026) states the SEC found that CS&Co. made false and misleading statements in Form ADV Part 2A brochures about the cash allocations in Schwab Intelligent Portfolios accounts, including about its conflict of interest in setting the cash allocations and the negative effect of the cash allocations on performance. Why it might matter: the order found CS&Co. and its former affiliate violated certain provisions of the Advisers Act from March 2015 through November 2018.

Trade press (August 26, 2026) reports the SEC has targeted advisors and firms in ongoing sweeps over misleading advertising, with wealth management firms cited for failing to comply with Rule 206(4)-1 (the Marketing Rule) governing how third-party ratings are used, including a September 2024 sweep settling against nine RIAs for a combined $1.24 million in fines. Why it might matter: the firms allegedly touted third-party ratings on their materials in non-compliance with the Marketing Rule.

FINRA's oversight materials (December 9, 2025) reference SEC Rule 606 of Regulation NMS disclosures on order handling and routing, including responses to frequently asked questions and a risk alert on observations related to Rule 606 disclosures. Why it might matter: the material reflects an SEC adoption of rules that increase information brokers must provide to investors on order handling.

Schwab's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that on June 12, 2025 the SEC withdrew certain notices of proposed rulemaking, including the December 2022 equity market structure rule proposals 'Order Competition Rule' and 'Regulation Best Execution', which the company had been evaluating. Why it might matter: the withdrawn proposals included equity market structure rules the company had been evaluating, alongside an FDIC withdrawal of certain proposals in March 2025.

Trade coverage (September 30, 2026) states the SEC's sustained focus on cash sweep disclosures, combined with litigation against major firms over allegedly low client yields on uninvested cash, is keeping cash sweep transparency and pricing a live compliance issue across the independent channel. Why it might matter: advisors should be prepared to explain how their custodian's sweep structure works and how it may shift with the rate environment.

Trade press (October 16, 2026) reports state securities regulators (NASAA) settled with Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch over charges of unreasonable commissions on small-dollar retail equity transactions, requiring a combined $4.4 million settlement with restitution on excess commissions over a five-year period. Why it might matter: the investigation was led by Massachusetts and joined by regulators in Alabama, Iowa, Missouri, Montana, New Jersey, and Texas.

Schwab (ADV, October 15, 2026) states it is required under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 to provide clients disclosure brochures describing how services work, the fees charged, and important conflicts of interest, and to update these brochures and notify clients of material changes. Why it might matter: the firm is also required to update these brochures from time to time and to notify clients when there are material changes, summarizing material changes in a Notice of Change.

Morgan Stanley's January 2017 SEC settlement order (dated January 13, 2017) found MSWM charged advisory fees in excess of what had been disclosed to and agreed to by clients, and failed to comply with custody examination and compliance requirements. Why it might matter: the SEC found that from 2009 through 2015, MSWM inadvertently charged advisory fees in excess of what had been disclosed to and agreed to by legacy clients of Citigroup Global Markets Inc., a predecessor to MSWM.

Schwab (2Q25 earnings call, July 18, 2025) notes the reduction of the SEC Section 31 fee rate to zero as a factor affecting 2025 expenses and transaction fees. Why it might matter: the source notes the SEC 31 fee rate reduction to zero was one factor, alongside elevated client engagement and transaction and related asset-level fees, in the firm's level of spending for 2025.

Morgan Stanley's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it has experienced, and may continue to experience, pricing pressures as competitors seek to gain market share by reducing prices and fees, paying higher deposit rates, eliminating commissions or offering more favorable terms. Why it might matter: certain competitors may be subject to different and, in some cases, less stringent, legal and regulatory regimes than the firm, thereby putting it at a competitive disadvantage.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states that regulatory requirements have produced greater price transparency, driving price competition and lower trading margins, and that competitors seek market share by cutting fees, commissions or margins. Why it might matter: trading margins have been further compressed by the shift from high- to low-touch services over time, which has created additional competitive pressure.

Schwab's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states increased price competition from other financial services firms to attract clients, including reduced commissions, higher deposit rates and reduced mutual fund or ETF expense ratios. Why it might matter: such price competition could impact the firm's results of operations and financial condition.

Edward Jones's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) notes competition from major brokerage firms offering zero commissions and lower cost, computer-based robo-advice. Why it might matter: clients can transfer their business to competing organizations at any time, and the partnership faces intense competition among firms to attract and retain clients.

Bank of America's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it faces increasing pressure to provide products and services on more attractive terms, including lower fees, lower cost investment strategies and higher deposit rates. Why it might matter: the firm may be disadvantaged by its size, the jurisdictions in which it is organized or operates, or by more stringent regulatory requirements applicable to it than to nonbank competitors.

McKinsey research (April 8, 2026) states fee pressure will be uneven, manifesting as demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: historically, fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019, even as digital tools have proliferated.

Deloitte (May 20, 2026) states that competitive pressure may compress fees as planning outputs become easier to compare. Why it might matter: lower cost-to-serve can expand margins for firms that execute and maintain pricing, creating margin expansion for some but pressure for others.

Morgan Stanley's CFO (2Q26 earnings call, July 15, 2026) was asked about press coverage of smaller RIAs employing more aggressive pricing to compete for workplace business. Why it might matter: the question focused on how the competitive landscape is evolving in workplace and steps to sustain higher client conversion rates.

A WealthTender survey (August 13, 2025) found nearly half (48%) of participants cited pricing and overall anticipated costs among the top three factors for choosing one advisor over another, framed as a need for transparent, reasonable pricing rather than the lowest cost. Why it might matter: transparent, reasonable pricing gives clients peace of mind and helps them budget.

Raymond James's 10-K (period ended September 30, 2025) states it competes with higher deposit rates to attract client cash balances, which could result in pricing pressure. Why it might matter: competition to attract clients or trading volume, through direct-to-investor online financial services, could result in pricing pressure or otherwise adversely impact the business.

Edward Jones's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it is subject to competition from robo-advisors and other lower cost options and fintech companies with internet- and mobile-based platforms. Why it might matter: if the partnership does not meet client needs, it could lose clients, thereby reducing revenues.

Bank of America's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states non-traditional providers and technology companies compete through electronic securities trading with low or no fees and commissions. Why it might matter: technologies and the growth of e-commerce have lowered geographic and monetary barriers, making it easier for non-depository institutions to offer traditional banking products and services.

Raymond James' CEO (1Q26 earnings call, April 22, 2026) states the firm wants a profitable, competitive and fair pricing structure and would evolve with competitive pressures, client preferences and industry dynamics on all pricing, fees and payout. Why it might matter: the firm looks at pricing, fees and payout on an ongoing basis, and would be flexible and open to evolving with where clients and advisors in the industry are evolving.

A survey (2025) found that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor, and pricing is the top factor in final advisor selection. Why it might matter: lack of fee transparency was identified as a red flag by 38% of survey participants.

A survey (2025) describes clear fee communication as a competitive advantage and a powerful differentiator, cited by 73% as a priority. Why it might matter: 'Fee structure and pricing' was cited by 61.8% of respondents as the most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor.

A survey (2025) found pricing and overall anticipated cost was the top factor (48.2%) in choosing one advisor over another. Why it might matter: 'Fee structure and pricing' was cited by 61.8% of respondents as the most helpful information when looking for a financial advisor.

Schwab's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states that its industry is highly competitive and characterized by aggressive price competition. Why it might matter: such events could result in material financial losses, legal or regulatory claims, and reputational harm, even if the firm is not at fault.

Morgan Stanley's 10-K (period ended December 31, 2025) states it competes on several factors including price, and that the financial services industry is intensely competitive. Why it might matter: the firm has experienced, and will likely continue to experience, increased competition driven by established financial services firms and emerging firms, including non-financial companies.

Sources (September 29, 2026) attribute new platform tolls and data fees at major distributors to the zeroing out of commissions in the brokerage industry, requiring revenue replacement. Why it might matter: distributors have real costs to distributing, and the revenue replacement has to come from somewhere if loads aren't being charged on funds.

An analyst (October 26, 2026) noted large team departures may be structural given attractive economics in RIA ownership, and that Ameriprise reportedly responded with cash retention bonuses and reductions to platform fees. Why it might matter: stronger recruiting and retention from the wirehouses has also slowed breakaways to IBDs.

A Wealthtender study of higher-income, decision-making adults (August 13, 2025) found that fee transparency is the highest-impact priority (73%) for advisors to address, and that economic stress might increase the importance of fee sensitivity. Why it might matter: the study also recommends online reputation (83% research reputation), response time (50% expect 24-48 hour response), and specialization clarity (64% want specialization info) as priorities.

The Wealthtender study (August 13, 2025) found that consumers prioritize fee transparency when selecting an advisor and expect good advisors to be transparent about their fees. Why it might matter: consumers are advised to plan to contact 2-3 advisors or more to compare options.

McKinsey (PriceMetrix, February 10, 2025) attributes stable to slightly increasing advisory fee rates partly to increasing demand for human advice, noting fee rates have stabilized after compression from 2013 to 2018. Why it might matter: among investors with more than $1 million in investable assets, the share willing to pay a premium of 100 basis points or more grew by 50 percent.

Cerulli (May 28, 2025) reports fee-based planning is the most preferred form of compensating an advisor among affluent investors, preferred by 36%. Why it might matter: clients have responded well to this shift given that their compensation is tied to portfolio performance rather than to selling particular products.

Schwab (1Q26 earnings call, April 16, 2026) states its business model is informed by investors' preferences for lower explicit fees without sacrificing product access, convenience, or service. Why it might matter: to the extent those preferences change at some point in the future, Schwab has flexibility to continue supporting investors and RIAs while still delivering strong returns for stockholders.

McKinsey research (April 8, 2026) holds that fee pressure in wealth management will be uneven, manifesting as client demands for transparency and unbundled pricing rather than a blanket reduction in basis points. Why it might matter: historically, fee rates for relationships of more than $1 million have remained remarkably steady at about 104 basis points since 2019, even as digital tools have proliferated.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (October 9, 2025) found that high-net-worth next-generation households seek transparency in advisor compensation, along with broader life guidance and emerging investment products. Why it might matter: advisors must adapt to these shifting dynamics to effectively serve the distinctive demands of this generation, which is navigating unique life stages and ambitious financial goals.

Vanguard research (June 4, 2025) found that for digital advice, key client attributes include the need for transparency (visibility of portfolio changes, fee awareness) and empowerment. Why it might matter: for human advice, value is mostly derived from a client's relationship with their financial advisor, whereas digital advice attributes differ.

Schwab (1Q26 deck, April 16, 2026) states that clients continue to choose the firm for its 'no trade-offs' approach to investing, combining value, service, trust and transparency. Why it might matter: Schwab offers an expanding set of investment solutions that support clients across every stage of their financial journey.

Schwab CEO Richard Wurster (1Q26 earnings call, April 16, 2026) stated that, according to research, more than half of the firm's clients are willing to pay for AI financial tools, which he said creates opportunities for new fee-based offers clients would be willing to pay for. Why it might matter: AI is already helping drive productivity across the firm, with every sales, service and advice professional using AI every day.

Raymond James (press release, July 22, 2026) reported record quarter-end Private Client Group assets in fee-based accounts of $1.15 trillion for June 30, 2026, up 22% over June 2025 and 11% over March 2026, with net inflows into PCG fee-based accounts. Why it might matter: record quarterly net revenues rose 14% year-over-year, primarily driven by higher asset management and related administrative fees.

Schwab's CEO (2Q25 earnings call, July 18, 2025) states the firm has been a leader in innovation for 50 years, always working alongside regulators in a way that creates transparency and low-cost, effective markets.

Schwab's CEO (3Q26 earnings call, October 15, 2026) states the firm makes it very easy and transparent for clients to see how much cash they hold and what other ways they could invest it, and that it will innovate around helping clients make those decisions.

Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Merrill has newly created two kinds of fees for third-party asset managers: data analytics fees (up to $1.4 million in incentives per year) and a basis-point revenue share (up to 0.1% on all Merrill assets a manager runs).

Merrill (ADV, October 30, 2026) discloses that receipt of data analytics fees from third-party firms creates conflicts of interest, giving it a financial incentive to make available and recommend products from firms that pay such fees.

Raymond James' CEO (1Q26 earnings call, April 22, 2026) states the firm wants a profitable, competitive and fair pricing structure for clients, financial professionals and the firm, and would be flexible and open to evolving with where the industry's clients and advisors are heading.

Merrill (ADV, October 30, 2026) states client assets in its Program are generally invested in the lowest cost eligible mutual fund share class, and that its advisors have no incentive to recommend higher-expense share classes because their compensation is not affected by share class selection.

Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Merrill Lynch is creating new revenue-sharing support fees and data/shelf fees for third-party asset managers to pay, with the support fee costing up to $1 million per $1 billion of assets managed on behalf of Merrill advisors, ranging from 0.02% on high-net-worth assets to a maximum 0.1% on third-party mutual funds, money market funds, and active ETFs.
Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Merrill Lynch is a laggard on data fees, being later than many of its peers which have sold advisor data for years, according to analyst Greg O'Gara.
Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Schwab was an early adopter (leading) on data fees, having introduced data fees over seven years ago.
Trade press (September 29, 2026) reports major wirehouses UBS and Wells Fargo introduced data fees in the mid-2010s and 2020, respectively, earlier than Merrill Lynch.

Trade press (October 16, 2026) reports Wells Fargo and Merrill Lynch agreed to a combined $4.4 million settlement with state securities regulators over charges of unreasonable commissions on small-dollar retail equity transactions (more than 256,000 transactions over a five-year period).

On the question of which firms are leading or lagging on fee structure changes and transparency, the comparison cannot be reliably made on this evidence: the definitions and bases are not unified across firms (fee-structure changes and transparency are reported as qualitative statements, unverified metrics, and firm-specific disclosures with differing scopes, periods, and quantities), so firms cannot be ranked on a single common basis. However, the evidence does contain directional, same-basis signals on data-fee timing: trade press (September 29, 2026) reports Schwab introduced data fees over seven years ago (an early adopter/leading), and that Merrill Lynch is later than many peers on data fees (a laggard).
